facts.title: Last of the Actinides
facts.text: Lawrencium, with atomic number 103, sits at the very end of the actinide series in the periodic table. As the final actinide, it bridges this f-block row to the transactinides that begin with rutherfordium (element 104). Its placement makes it a key marker for testing chemical periodicity in the heaviest elements.

facts.title: Named for the Cyclotron Pioneer
facts.text: The element honors Ernest O. Lawrence, the American physicist who invented the cyclotron particle accelerator in 1931 and won the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics. The same Lawrence lends his name to two U.S. national laboratories, Lawrence Berkeley and Lawrence Livermore. Its symbol was originally 'Lw' before being changed to 'Lr' by IUPAC in 1963.

facts.title: A Cold War Discovery Dispute
facts.text: Lawrencium was first reported in 1961 by a team led by Albert Ghiorso at the Lawrence Berkeley laboratory in California. A Soviet group at Dubna also made claims to its discovery in the 1960s, fueling a Cold War priority dispute. IUPAC and IUPAP eventually credited both Berkeley and Dubna with shared roles in confirming the element.

facts.title: It Vanishes in Hours
facts.text: Lawrencium has no stable isotopes; every form is radioactive and short-lived. Its longest-lived isotope, lawrencium-266, has a half-life of only about 11 hours, while most others decay in seconds or minutes. This fleeting existence means scientists must study it within moments of creating it.

facts.title: Made an Atom at a Time
facts.text: Lawrencium does not occur in nature and can only be produced artificially in particle accelerators. It is made by bombarding targets of elements like californium or americium with light ions such as boron or oxygen nuclei. Only a few atoms have ever been created at once, making bulk samples impossible.

facts.title: An Electron Out of Place
facts.text: Lawrencium is predicted to have an unusual ground-state electron configuration ending in 7s2 7p1, rather than the 6d1 that simple patterns might suggest. This anomaly arises from relativistic effects, where the heavy nucleus accelerates inner electrons to a large fraction of light speed and reshuffles energy levels. It makes lawrencium a fascinating test case for relativistic quantum chemistry.

facts.title: The Easiest Electron to Remove
facts.text: In 2015, an international team working in Japan measured lawrencium's first ionization energy as roughly 4.96 electron volts. This is one of the lowest ionization energies of any element, reflecting that loosely bound 7p electron predicted by theory. The experiment was a landmark, directly probing the chemistry of an element available only as single atoms.

facts.title: Prefers the +3 State
facts.text: Like most actinides, lawrencium's most stable and characteristic oxidation state in solution is +3. Studies of its aqueous chemistry suggest its ionic radius and behavior fit smoothly into the trends of the heavier actinides. This consistency helps chemists confirm that the actinide series genuinely ends at element 103.

facts.title: Purely a Research Element
facts.text: Lawrencium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications whatsoever. Because only a handful of atoms can be made and they decay almost immediately, it exists solely as a subject of fundamental scientific research. Its value lies entirely in what it teaches us about the structure of matter at the edge of the periodic table.

facts.title: A Window Into Atomic Limits
facts.text: Studying lawrencium helps scientists understand how relativistic effects increasingly distort chemistry as nuclei grow heavier and more crowded with protons. These insights guide predictions about even heavier superheavy elements and the theorized 'island of stability.' In this way, a barely-existing element illuminates the rules that govern all atoms.
